verdict:
This is a small, precise, devastating novel about a handwritten document about abortion aftercare that traveled by hand through underground networks in communist Romania in 1984 — and about how a single formatting error, made in twenty minutes in a coal cellar by the woman who wrote it, cost a nineteen-year-old named Ana Petrescu her life. The book never tells you to feel anything. It shows you the mechanism and trusts you to arrive at the feeling on your own. This restraint is its greatest strength, and — in one significant place — its greatest limitation.

Three voices carry the story: Ilinca, the bookkeeper who authored the document and made the fatal copy; Doina, the nineteen-year-old factory worker who received a copy from a stranger on a bus; and Munteanu, the investigator assigned to trace the paper's path. The prose is different for each of them without ever calling attention to itself. Ilinca thinks in accounting language — "confirmed figures," "open columns," "provisional entries" — and this vocabulary gradually becomes the book's emotional grammar: when Ilinca says a column is "still open," we feel the weight of that open column. Doina is watchful and funny in a dry way and terrified in a way she doesn't name. Munteanu is thorough and fair in the particular way that makes him more frightening, not less: he does good detective work and the outcome is still terrible.

The first nine chapters are as gripping as anything I've read in recent historical fiction. The procedural detective work — Munteanu laying two copies side by side, noticing that "by the bed" and "beside the bed" represent two separate hands each copying from a third original — produces genuine intellectual excitement. And the moment in chapter 9 when Ilinca reads the corrupted version of her own document and understands exactly what happened is about as perfect as endings of chapters get.

Chapters 10 through 18 slow considerably. Ilinca's branch-tracing — the pharmacy visit, the bread-delivery relay, the bread-queue acquaintance, the canteen overheard conversation — follows the same basic structure four or five times in succession: indirect contact, message passed, node confirmed. The writing remains beautiful sentence by sentence, but the narrative tension plateaus. I started reading faster somewhere in chapter 13 and didn't come back to full attention until chapter 18 (Doina brought in for questioning), which snapped the story forward again.

Chapters 22 through 30 are extraordinary. The moment when Ilinca reads the nine on the cellar woman's page — confirming what she has feared for five weeks — is followed by the reconstruction, in chapter 24, of exactly how the error happened: the light coming from the upper right, the bracket's bottom horizontal in shadow, the column procedure moving her hand forward to write the next numeral before her eyes had finished reading the margin. It's the most precise account I've ever read of how a careful person makes a mistake. And then Ilinca's walk to the station with both documents — one in each pocket — is as quietly brave a thing as I've seen in a novel, all the more so because the book refuses to call it brave.

The last chapter is perfect. Doina stands on the station steps and recites the document from memory, bracket and all, the pigeons indifferent, the fog on the Someș. "There is no way to draw a bracket in memory. What you have instead is the space where the bracket was." That's the whole book in one sentence.

There are real problems. Ana Petrescu — the person at the center of everything — never exists as a person. Her death is procedurally established in chapter 4 and emotionally referenced throughout, but we never see her, never hear her voice, never feel the texture of her life. The book's formal restraint, usually a strength, becomes a wall here. When Doina says near the end that she thinks about Ana "as long as I can hold the thought before it tips into something I can't do anything useful with," the reader knows exactly what she means — because we, too, have nothing of Ana but a name and a record. That's a political truth about how the system treated her, but it's also a craft limitation. A nineteen-year-old died. I believe it. I did not feel it. The book deserved to solve that problem and doesn't.

There are also three smaller technical problems. The "Wash and keep" / "Keep and wash" reversal in Doina's copy versus Ilinca's original exists clearly in the text (chapter 9 versus chapter 14) but is never noted by any character — not Munteanu, who is obsessively attentive to every other variant, and not Doina or Ilinca. Given how carefully the book documents every other drift between copies, this silence reads as an oversight. Separately, chapter 30 has Doina state that Ana "died in the morning," but the hospital record established in chapter 4 gives the time of death as 23:12 — late evening, not morning. This may be intentional unreliable narration (Doina has only hearsay knowledge), but the sentence's rhetorical structure — "the paper said *in the morning* and she died in the morning" — presents it as known fact. Finally, the address confusion around Dorobanților versus Strada Crișan (Munteanu's notebook has one address from Viorica Damian's interview; the population register gives another) is eventually explained but so implicitly, and across so many chapters, that it will confuse careful readers tracking the investigation.

strongest.claim: The central conceit — that a formatting distinction (bracket versus numbered ninth line) is both the book's moral heart and its plot engine — is wholly original and wholly earned. The distance between a bracket and a nine is the distance between 'do not wait for the morning' and 'in the morning,' and the book traces that distance across thirty-one days and nine women's hands without ever losing it.

The three narrators are completely distinct — Ilinca's accounting language, Doina's precise dry watchfulness, Munteanu's methodical fairness — and the transitions between them never blur. Reading one immediately calls up the texture of the other two.

Munteanu's document analysis — particularly in chapters 8 and 16 — is genuinely exciting procedural work. The deduction that two copies drifting in the same direction prove a shared source they've each diverged from is elementary philology rendered as detective fiction, and it works beautifully.

Chapter 24 (The Light from the Door) is the emotional and intellectual climax: Ilinca reconstructs, in real time, exactly how she wrote a nine in the coal cellar when she meant to draw a bracket. The reconstruction is so precise — the angle of the light, the column procedure, the hand moving before the eye had finished — that the reader understands both the inevitability of the error and its full cost.

The final chapter is flawless. Doina on the station steps, reciting the document from memory including the bracket, concluding with 'the bracket included.' The irony that her perfectly memorized version carries its own inherited mutation ('each hour' instead of 'every') is the book's deepest note, sounded once and never explained.

weakest.claim: Ana Petrescu never exists as a person. She is a record, a name, a procedure. This is partly a deliberate formal choice (she is dead before the book begins; the system treats her as a case), but the restraint becomes a limitation: a nineteen-year-old died and the reader is told this repeatedly without ever feeling it. The book earns its grief on everything except the person who should be at its center.

Chapters 13–17 follow an essentially identical rhythm — Ilinca finds an indirect route (pharmacy acquaintance, bread-delivery relay, bread-queue contact, canteen overheard conversation), sends a message, receives confirmation — four or five times without significant tonal variation. The branch-tracing is necessary to the plot, but the repetition of structure creates a plateau in tension precisely where the novel most needs to be building.

The 'Wash and keep' / 'Keep and wash' reversal between Ilinca's master (chapter 9) and Doina's copy (chapter 14) is a meaningful textual mutation — it shows Doina's branch has its own drift from the original — but it is never noticed or noted by any character, including Munteanu, who is obsessively attentive to every other variant. Given the book's formal premise, this silence reads as an authorial oversight.

Chapter 30 states that Ana Petrescu 'died in the morning,' but the hospital record established in chapter 4 gives the time of death as twenty-three hundred and twelve — late evening, not morning. This may be intended as Doina's imperfect secondhand knowledge, but the sentence presents it as known fact within a chapter that is otherwise carefully precise.

The Dorobanților / Strada Crișan address discrepancy — Munteanu's notebook has Dorobanților (from Viorica Damian's interview in chapter 12), but the cellar woman's registered address is on Strada Crișan (discovered via the Population Section in chapter 25) — is eventually resolved but so implicitly that readers carefully tracking the investigation across chapters 12 through 25 will be confused. The November 29th 'Dorobanților visit' that goes nowhere is mentioned but never shown.

quotes.text: Lines one through eight: hers. Correct. Line nine: not hers. The error is in the being careful.
quotes.why: This is the novel's thesis in three sentences. It earns its precision because the reader has spent nine chapters watching Ilinca be careful. The reversal — 'the error is in the being careful' — lands like a verdict.

quotes.text: Both of these documents had tried to be the same as some third thing — something they had each been copied from — and both had succeeded, and each had arrived at something slightly different from the other.
quotes.why: Munteanu's deduction that two copies drifting in the same direction prove a common source is textual criticism rendered as detective work. The sentence is also the book's epistemological premise: you find the original by studying its imperfect copies.

quotes.text: She was in the procedure of the column and the ninth element is outside the procedure and she did not stop for the element that was outside it.
quotes.why: This is the exact mechanism of the error, stated with the precision of a final audit. A competent-but-ordinary line would say 'she made a mistake.' This line says something unreachable by ordinary prose: that the mistake was produced by the very procedure that made her good at her work.

quotes.text: The woman who gave it to me had a face like a closed shop and she put it in my hand the way you pass someone the salt — without asking if they wanted salt, without looking at them while they took it.
quotes.why: The simile does several things at once: it establishes the impersonality that keeps both women safe, the practiced ease of a woman who has done this before, and the mundane domesticity that the novel insists is the appropriate register for what these women are risking.

quotes.text: There is no way to draw a bracket in memory. What you have instead is the space where the bracket was
quotes.why: This is the book's final irony stated as simple fact: Doina preserves the document but cannot preserve the bracket's form, only its function — the pause, the override, the instruction that says the sequence ends here. It also describes what the reader is left with: not the bracket, but the space where it was.

put_down_points: Chapter 13 (The Bloc Woman): the fourth indirect-relay sequence in succession. After the pharmacy, the bread delivery, and the bread-queue contact, a reader who needs narrative forward motion starts moving through this one faster. The structure is not wrong — it is the correct portrayal of how Ilinca must work — but four iterations is one too many for a reader who does not already trust the payoff.

Chapter 17 (Nine or Bracket): the longest of the branch-tracing chapters, in which Ilinca tilts the original under the lamp and understands that she probably wrote a nine. This is an important realization, but the chapter arrives after several chapters of the same rhythm and before the confirmation in chapter 22, leaving it in an awkward middle position where the book is neither building nor resolving.
who_is_this_for: Readers who responded to the formal architecture of A Gentleman in Moscow, the historical compression of Suite Française, or the procedural patience of HHhH. Anyone who cares about women's underground networks under oppressive regimes and is willing to inhabit three different consciousness-types without a conventional plot driving them forward. This is not a book for someone who needs a warm protagonist or a cathartic release — the emotional payoff is real but it arrives in the mode of recognition, not catharsis. The book club member who will love it is the one who says, at the end of the evening, "I keep thinking about the bracket." The one who will resist it is the one who spent the middle wondering when something was going to happen.
